tasks.description: Get today's date and now's datetime. Print both. Also print just the year, month, and day from today.
tasks.hint:
`from datetime import date, datetime`
`date.today()` → current date; `datetime.now()` → current date AND time.
Access parts: `today.year`, `today.month`, `today.day`
tasks.solution:
from datetime import date, datetime

today = date.today()
now = datetime.now()

print(f'Today: {today}')
print(f'Now: {now}')
print(f'Year: {today.year}, Month: {today.month}, Day: {today.day}')
tasks.walkthrough:
`date.today()` gives the calendar date and `datetime.now()` gives the date with the current time.
The individual parts are plain integers available as attributes.

tasks.description: Create a `date` for your birthday. Calculate how many days until/since your next birthday.
tasks.hint:
`birthday = date(year, month, day)` — pick any year for the date object.
Subtract dates: `date1 - date2` returns a `timedelta` object.
`delta.days` gives the number of days as an integer.
tasks.solution:
from datetime import date

today = date.today()
birthday = date(today.year, 6, 15)

if birthday < today:
    birthday = date(today.year + 1, 6, 15)

days_until = (birthday - today).days
print(f'Days until next birthday: {days_until}')
tasks.walkthrough:
The birthday is built for this year first. If it has already passed, it's rebuilt for next year.
Subtracting today from it gives a timedelta, and `.days` extracts the count. Change the month and day to your own.

tasks.description: Use `strftime` to format today's date as: 'Monday, 26 May 2025'. Also use `strptime` to parse '2025-12-25' back to a date.
tasks.hint:
`date.today().strftime('%A, %d %B %Y')` formats the date.
Format codes: `%A` = full weekday, `%d` = day, `%B` = full month, `%Y` = 4-digit year.
`datetime.strptime('2025-12-25', '%Y-%m-%d')` parses a string into a datetime.
tasks.solution:
from datetime import date, datetime

today = date.today()
print(today.strftime('%A, %d %B %Y'))

parsed = datetime.strptime('2025-12-25', '%Y-%m-%d')
print(parsed.date())
print(parsed.strftime('%A'))
tasks.walkthrough:
`strftime` turns a date into text using the format codes: full weekday name, day, full month name, year.
`strptime` does the reverse, reading text with a matching format into a datetime. Calling `.date()` on it drops the time part.

tasks.description: Use `timedelta` to find the date 90 days from today and 30 days ago.
tasks.hint:
`from datetime import timedelta`
`date.today() + timedelta(days=90)` → 90 days in the future.
`date.today() - timedelta(days=30)` → 30 days in the past.
tasks.solution:
from datetime import date, timedelta

today = date.today()
print(f'Today: {today}')
print(f'In 90 days: {today + timedelta(days=90)}')
print(f'30 days ago: {today - timedelta(days=30)}')
tasks.walkthrough: A `timedelta` is a duration. Adding it moves forward, subtracting moves back, and month and year boundaries are handled correctly.

tasks.description: Measure how long a piece of code takes using `datetime.now()` before and after running it.
tasks.hint:
`start = datetime.now()`
Run your code (e.g. a loop that counts to 1 million).
`elapsed = datetime.now() - start` → a timedelta object.
`elapsed.total_seconds()` gives the time in seconds as a float.
tasks.solution:
from datetime import datetime

start = datetime.now()

total = 0
for i in range(1_000_000):
    total += i

elapsed = datetime.now() - start
print(f'Total: {total}')
print(f'Took {elapsed.total_seconds():.4f} seconds')
tasks.walkthrough:
Two timestamps bracket the work. Their difference is a timedelta, and `total_seconds()` gives it as a float.
For serious timing, `time.perf_counter()` is more precise, but this works fine for a rough idea.

lesson.intro:
Dates are harder than they look: months have different lengths, years leap,
and "30 days from now" needs care. The `datetime` module handles all of that.
Today: getting the current date and time, doing arithmetic with `timedelta`,
and converting to and from text.

sections.heading: date and datetime
sections.body:
`date.today()` is just the calendar date. `datetime.now()` is date plus
time. Both have `.year`, `.month`, `.day`; datetime adds `.hour`,
`.minute`, `.second`.
sections.code:
from datetime import date, datetime

today = date.today()
now = datetime.now()
print(today)
print(now)
print(today.year, today.month, today.day)

sections.heading: Subtracting dates gives a timedelta
sections.body:
Subtract two dates and you get a `timedelta`, a length of time. Its
`.days` is an integer you can print or compare.
sections.code:
from datetime import date

birthday = date(2026, 12, 25)
until = birthday - date(2026, 9, 15)
print(until)
print(until.days)

sections.heading: Adding a timedelta moves a date
sections.body:
`timedelta(days=90)` is a duration. Add it to or subtract it from a date
to move forwards or backwards, and month boundaries are handled for you.
sections.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta

start = date(2026, 9, 15)
print(start + timedelta(days=90))
print(start - timedelta(days=30))
print(start + timedelta(weeks=2))

sections.heading: strftime and strptime
sections.body:
`strftime` formats a date as text using codes: `%A` weekday name, `%d`
day, `%B` month name, `%Y` four-digit year, `%m` month number. `strptime`
parses text back into a datetime using the same codes.
sections.code:
from datetime import date, datetime

d = date(2025, 5, 26)
print(d.strftime('%A, %d %B %Y'))
print(d.strftime('%d/%m/%Y'))

parsed = datetime.strptime('2025-12-25', '%Y-%m-%d')
print(parsed.date())

sections.heading: Timing code
sections.body:
Subtracting two `datetime.now()` calls gives a timedelta;
`.total_seconds()` turns it into a float.
sections.code:
from datetime import datetime

start = datetime.now()
total = sum(range(1_000_000))
elapsed = datetime.now() - start
print(f'{elapsed.total_seconds():.3f} seconds')

watch_out: `import datetime` vs `from datetime import datetime`: the module and the class share a name. With the first form it's `datetime.datetime.now()`.
`strptime` needs the format to match the text exactly, separators included.
You can't subtract a `date` from a `datetime` directly. Use `.date()` on the datetime first.
`timedelta` has no months or years, because their length varies.
